Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}

Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Travail de recherche : utilise EXACTEMENT ces intertitres, dans cet ordre : « La question » (pourquoi ce travail, d'après l'introduction) ; « Les conclusions » (principaux résultats, avec les chiffres) ; « La méthode » (données et démarche, en quelques phrases) ; « Ce que ça implique » (explication accessible des conséquences, telles que les auteurs les présentent) ; « Les limites » (uniquement celles mentionnées par les auteurs ; omets cette section s'ils n'en mentionnent aucune). Remplis « reference » : auteurs, institution ou revue, date, et nature du document (document de travail non relu par des pairs, article de revue à comité de lecture, billet de chercheur…), uniquement d'après le texte fourni.

Coase Meets Negishi: Property Rights, Welfare Weights, and Distributional Consequences
in Climate Economics
Simon F. Lang, Matthew D. Gordon, and Matthew J. Kotchen
NBER Working Paper No. 35971
October 2026
JEL No. H41, Q50
ABSTRACT
We develop a property-rights based approach for defining welfare weights in economic models of 
climate change. Whether there is a "right to pollute" or a "right to no pollution" is increasingly 
contested in legislatures, courts, and international climate negotiations. We show how these notions 
of property rights can provide the basis for "Coasean welfare weights" that are applicable in 
multilateral public goods settings. Distributional questions are addressed through positive analysis, 
conditional on property rights, rather than normative views about redistribution. The implied 
transfers are consistent with a bargained solution over the net benefits of addressing climate change 
and reflect the value of property rights over emissions. The approach defines efficient allocations 
that generate Pareto improvements, in contrast to commonly used Negishi weights. We implement 
the approach in a global integrated assessment model to quantify what countries have at stake in 
ongoing political and legal debates about emissions-related property rights.

1 Introduction
A large and growing body of evidence shows that climate change will cause substantial and
highly uneven damages across countries (e.g., Diaz, 2016; Carleton et al., 2022; Hultgren et
al., 2025). Less attention has been given to the way that resolving climate change through
collective action will also have distributional consequences. These consequences arise not
only because of heterogeneity in avoided damages across countries, but also because of dif-
ferences in abatement costs and the extent to which international transfers may (or may not)
occur. Resolving climate change among countries is at its core a global public goods prob-
lem (Barrett, 2007; Buchholz and Sandler, 2021), and a seminal insight of Samuelson (1954)
is that public goods problems do not, in general, have a unique Pareto efficient solution.
Instead, there is a set of efficient allocations that differ in their distributional consequences.
Solving public goods problems, such as climate change, therefore requires selecting among
allocations on the basis of some criterion beyond efficiency, and how economists make this
choice remains an enduring source of debate.
The choice is typically framed as the need for analysts to choose welfare weights across
countries or regions for use in a global planner’s social welfare function (Dietz, 2024). A
common approach is to use a variant of Negishi weights, where the resulting Pareto efficient
allocation is the one that arises without international transfers (Nordhaus and Yang, 1996;
Manne and Richels, 2005; Leimbach et al., 2010; Krusell and Smith Jr., 2022; Traeger, 2023;
Alsina-Pujols, 2026). The approach is often understood as allowing analysts to separate the
problem of climate change from global income inequality, addressing the inefficiency of cli-
mate change while sidestepping normative judgments about distributional justice (Nordhaus
and Yang, 1996; Hassler and Krusell, 2012; Barrage, 2020). This interpretation is nev-
ertheless criticized for failing to recognize implicit normative assumptions (Stanton, 2011;
Kelleher, 2018). The main alternative in the literature is more explicitly normative, whereby
analysts use social welfare functions with some degree of inequality aversion (Chichilnisky
and Heal, 1994; Tol, 1997, 2002; Dennig et al., 2015; Budolfson et al., 2021; Lang, 2026).
These social welfare functions introduce a redistributive motive, but critics of the approach
argue that the implied transfers may require more international redistribution than countries
are willing to undertake. 1
This paper develops a novel alternative: welfare weights derived from a positive analysis

2022; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2023; Conte et al., 2026; Hassler et al., 2026) and others using

1
of property rights and bargaining, rather than either an assumption of zero transfers or an
imposed criterion of distributional equity. The lack of well-defined property rights is a key
feature of public goods problems. There are, however, ongoing debates among policymak-
ers and in the courts over attempts to establish the “right to pollute” or the “right to no
pollution” with respect to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. We show how these standard
notions of property rights can provide the basis for what we refer to as Coasean welfare
weights. Use of these weights results in efficient allocations that feature transfer payments
between countries. But importantly, the transfers are not driven by normative views about
global redistribution. Instead, the transfers represent the outcome of a hypothetical bargain
over the distribution of surplus obtained by implementing an efficient resolution of climate
change, conditional on assignment of property rights. Beyond providing a conceptual basis
for Coasean welfare weights, we apply them in a calibrated integrated assessment model
(IAM) of global climate change. The quantitative analysis compares the distributional con-
sequences of different allocations and shows what countries or regions have at stake when it
comes to questions about emissions-related property rights.
Property rights linked to climate change are increasingly debated and contested in courts,
legislatures, and international bodies around the world. In 2025, the International Court
of Justice issued an advisory opinion that countries should be held liable for their GHG
emissions.2 Citizens in a number of countries have sued governments and companies for not
doing enough to reduce emissions. 3 In the United States, municipalities have sued fossil-fuel
companies over liability for climate damages, and several states have enacted or proposed
“Climate Superfund” laws that mandate payment for damages or adaptation costs, though
the federal government is challenging these cases and laws in court. 4 Finally, international
transfers motivated by liability through “loss and damage” payments have become central
to international climate negotiations (UNFCCC, 2015, 2023, 2024).
Despite the increasing salience of questions about property rights, the topic has received
relatively little attention among economists regarding how it might affect the design of cli-
mate policy. In this paper, we use an intentionally simple theoretical model to illustrate
the fundamental ideas of our approach. We consider a static setting where each country’s

emissions generate a global public bad. Countries can differ according to domestic welfare
functions, initial endowments, benefits from their own emissions, and damages from aggre-

tion. For example, under “right to pollute,” the reference allocation is the Nash equilibrium,
since each country is free to emit and chooses its unilaterally optimal level of emissions. In
contrast, under “right to no pollution,” the reference allocation is zero emissions, since each
country has the right to prevent the emissions of all other countries. A key feature of the
setup—unlike standard externality settings with the potential for Coasean bargaining—is
that all countries are potential emitters, experiencing both benefits and costs. This means
that property rights are not clearly assigned to one set of countries or the other, but rather,
to the actions all countries may undertake.
A Coasean solution is then obtained through Nash (1950) bargaining, which defines a
particular Pareto efficient allocation, conditional on a given property-rights regime. The allo-
cation is consistent with what countries might choose for themselves through a decentralized
and cooperative bargaining procedure in the absence of transaction costs (Rubinstein, 1982;
Osborne and Rubinstein, 1990). The Coasean welfare weights consistent with this allocation
take a similar form to Negishi weights—the inverse of the marginal utility of consumption—
but in this case, the levels of consumption depend on transfer payments that reflect the
bargained value of the property rights over emissions. We describe how the resulting trans-
fers accord with a version of the beneficiary pays principle for emissions reductions under
“right to pollute,” and the polluter pays principle for emissions increases under “right to no
pollution.”
A key result is that Coasean welfare weights always result in a Pareto improvement
relative to the corresponding reference allocation, that is, all countries are made (weakly)
better off. This feature of the planner’s solution is important because the distributional
consequences of resolving climate change are central to the design and political feasibility
of international policy. In contrast, Pareto improvements do not necessarily arise with the
use of Negishi weights, highlighting their distributional consequences despite their frequent
interpretation as being distributionally neutral. We also use our model to identify conditions
under which a specific country will make or receive a transfer with Coasean welfare weights,
along with the conditions that dictate whether a country prefers one property-rights regime
over another.
We use calibrated simulations to illustrate use of Coasean welfare weights and quantify
the distributional consequences of different property-rights regimes. We develop a static IAM
that draws on RICE (Nordhaus and Yang, 1996) and C-DICE (Nordhaus, 2015). Focusing
first on the property-rights based reference allocations, we find that changing property rights
3
does not meaningfully change inequality across countries, yet it does meaningfully change
the level of consumption for certain countries. For example, moving from “right to pollute”
to “right to no pollution” causes consumption per capita to increase 15% in Sub-Saharan
Africa and decrease 9% in South Africa, while changes in the United States and the European
Union are less than 2%. These results imply that changing property rights is not, on its own,
fundamentally redistributive in a way that reorders consumption across countries, yet the
value of these rights can still be significant for some countries.
When comparing efficient allocations, distributional differences are interpreted as the
relative value of property rights conditional on successful Nash bargaining to a cooperative
solution. We find that, under “right to pollute,” the efficient allocation features total an-
nual transfers of$190 billion, whereas under “right to no pollution,” total transfers amount
to$1.03 trillion. Intuitively, countries with large benefits of emissions relative to climate
damages prefer “right to pollute” (e.g., Russia, South Africa, China, and Eurasia), whereas
countries with large climate damages relative to the benefits of emissions prefer “right to
no pollution” (e.g., Sub-Saharan Africa, Brazil, and a large set of other Asian countries).
Finally, by comparing reference allocations for one property-rights regime with the efficient
allocation for another, we show why countries may sometimes prefer to contest property
rights rather than address climate change. In particular, we illustrate how some countries
prefer the inefficient allocation under one set of property rights to the efficient allocation
under the alternative set.
The overarching contribution of this paper is to show how the choice of welfare weights in
climate economics can be grounded in a positive analysis of property rights. The approach
differs fundamentally from the use of inequality-averse social welfare functions and associated
equity weights, which impose a normative criterion of distributive equity. While we do not
prescribe how property rights should be assigned, we note that the choice itself is actively
debated and has normative content (Fleurbaey, 2008). Nevertheless, separating considera-
tion of the distributional consequences of property rights from questions about efficiency is
familiar territory for analysts of environmental and natural resource problems (Coase, 1960;
Libecap, 1990; Deryugina et al., 2021).
The approach is also distinct from the standard use of Negishi weights in climate models,
though we argue it is more closely aligned with Negishi’s original formulation with respect to
the role of initial endowments. Negishi’s (1960) original analysis applies to a private-goods
economy with no market failures, showing a correspondence between the decentralized equi-
librium and the appropriately weighted planner’s problem. When applied in climate models,
however, the public goods market failure is central, and Negishi weights are typically used
to implement an efficient allocation with an assumed no-transfer rule (e.g., Nordhaus and
4
Yang, 1996). But this rule ignores the distributional consequences based on heterogeneous
benefits and costs of addressing climate change, that is, efficient provision of the global pub-
lic good. Our approach differs in that the public good problem is addressed conceptually by
assigning property rights and modeling a decentralized bargaining procedure. The approach
thus represents a synthesis of Coasean logic with Negishi’s insight that welfare weights can
be chosen to support a decentralized allocation, conditional on a set of endowments. 5
Our analysis also relates to other strands of the literature. Existing studies examine the
way that international environmental agreements can be used to infer implied social welfare
weights (Eyckmans et al., 1993; Narita et al., 2010). The extensive literature on emissions
trading systems is founded on the notion of establishing partial property rights over the
“right to pollute” and allowing agents to buy and sell those rights (e.g., Montgomery, 1972;
Tietenberg, 1985; Nordhaus, 1991). A number of papers analyze Nash bargaining solutions
to climate change (Howarth, 1996; Tol, 1997; Yang, 2013; Yu et al., 2017; Tulkens, 2019;
Yang, 2020), but they consider only the Nash equilibrium as an initial allocation, without
explicit consideration of property rights. Finally, while the “right to no pollution” is less
studied, Ambec and Ehlers (2016) consider the welfare consequences of polluter-pays liability
as the basis for regulation in a multilateral setting, and recent papers by Tavoni et al. (2024)
and Burke et al. (2026) estimate loss and damage compensation payments based on historical
emissions and the SCC.
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 outlines the basic setup
of our theoretical model. Section 3 provides background on and discussion of the standard
approach to Negishi weights in climate models. Section 4 develops our property-rights based
approach, providing a formal definition of Coasean welfare weights and a discussion of the
implications. Section 5 outlines the setup of our climate-economy IAM and reports quanti-
tative results. Section 6 concludes with a brief summary and directions for future research.

5.4 Comparing reference and efficient allocations
Having made comparisons between reference allocations in Section 5.2 and between efficient
allocations in Section 5.3, we now compare reference and efficient allocations. Specifically, we
consider the resulting Pareto improvements (or lack thereof) when moving from a reference
allocation to an efficient allocation, both within and across property-rights regimes.
A key feature of using Coasean welfare weights, as highlighted in Proposition 1, is that
moving from a property-rights based reference allocation to the corresponding efficient allo-

6 Conclusion
This paper develops a property-rights based approach for defining welfare weights in cli-
mate economics. We show how familiar notions of the “right to pollute” or the “right to
no pollution” can provide the basis for Coasean welfare weights. The approach anchors
questions about distributional outcomes among countries in a positive analysis, conditional
on property rights, rather than on normative principles of distributional justice. Transfers
that arise among countries are not driven by a redistributive motive that a global planner
imposes. Instead, they follow the logic of Coasean bargaining, adapted to a multilateral
public goods setting, in accordance with the principles of either the “beneficiary pays” for
emissions reductions, or the “polluter pays” for emissions increases. In contrast to standard
approaches for choosing welfare weights in the literature, our approach obtains a globally
efficient allocation that is always a Pareto improvement for all countries, making the solution
potentially appealing among sovereign countries.
The framework is novel in the way it connects the insights of several seminal contributions.
Samuelson (1954) identifies the initial problem with the inherent need for welfare weights
when choosing among Pareto efficient allocations involving provision of a public good. Coase
(1960) shows how establishing property rights can resolve externality problems, and we
show how the same logic can apply to the global public goods problem of climate change,
with property rights over the right to pollute or not. We then show how Nash (1950)
bargaining identifies a particular Coasean solution, and calibrating Negishi (1960) weights
to the resulting Pareto efficient level of consumption in each country defines a corresponding
global social welfare function for potential use in IAMs.
The fundamental difference between Coasean welfare weights and Negishi weights as
commonly used in climate economics (e.g., Nordhaus and Yang, 1996) is the level of con-
sumption to which the weights are calibrated. Both approaches respect the initial distri-
bution of private-good endowments. The standard Negishi approach imposes a constraint
of no transfers among countries, yet as we make clear, distributional consequences arise
because countries differ in the net benefits of changes in emissions. In contrast, Coasean
welfare weights imply transfers among countries, but importantly, they are consistent with
a decentralized, Pareto-improving bargaining procedure. The standard Negishi approach is
often justified as the only way for IAMs to address climate change without simultaneously
addressing global income inequality. Our approach, however, provides an alternative, where
transfers reflect the value of property rights, rather than normative views about inequality.
At the same time, the resulting allocations still depend in part on the initial distribution
of endowments, as with Negishi weights, and to the extent there are equity concerns with
32
initial endowments, there may be equity concerns with the resulting efficient allocations.
We employ a relatively simple IAM and begin to quantify what countries (or regions)
have at stake in ongoing debates about emissions-related property rights. While the total
transfers that arise under either property-rights regime are not large enough to materi-
ally change the distribution of wealth across countries, the magnitudes are large enough to
have meaningful effects for certain countries. Underlying many of the results is the way
that countries with large benefits of emissions relative to climate damages tend to prefer
“right to pollute,” whereas countries with large climate damages relative to the benefits of
emissions tend to prefer “right to no pollution.” Cross-country heterogeneity and the result-
ing distributional consequences of alternative property-rights regimes help to explain why
climate-related property rights are sparking growing debate around the world.
Finally, we acknowledge that our quantitative application is relatively simple in order to
focus on the fundamental ideas, and future research can further clarify the consequences of
Coasean welfare weights compared to other approaches using more detailed IAMs. A natural
next step is to implement the approach in a dynamic IAM, one that captures the intertem-
poral nature of climate change and the potential value of property rights. We also focus
throughout on the Nash bargaining solution to simulate a decentralized Coasean bargain-
ing procedure, but alternative solution concepts might be worth considering in future work
(e.g., other bargaining approaches or definitions of core stability). Additionally, we consider
reference allocations based solely on RP and RnP, but our framework could accommodate
other considerations too, such as historical or differentiated responsibilities among countries.
Future research might also consider more explicit links to climate policy instruments, as
we focus on efficient allocations without regard to policies needed to implement them. For
example, one approach would be to implement globally efficient carbon taxes combined with
international transfers, but another is an emissions trading system with a particular alloca-
tion of permits that reflects the endowments implied here. In these settings, Coasean welfare
weights can be used to characterize specific Pareto-improving policy packages.
